newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka plantation firms near deal with labour.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka plantation firms near deal with labour.

text.p: Management companies running Sri Lanka's tea, rubber and coconut plantations are nearing a deal with a powerful labour union on a collective agreement, industry officials said on Thursday.
"We have a few more things to iron out," said Sene Seneviratne, director-general of the Planters' Association of Ceylon, which represents the management firms.
"We should reach an agreement very shortly. We realise worker participation is very important," he told Reuters.
Management companies already have a deal with the Ceylon Workers' Congress (CWC) union to freeze wages to December 1997, as a prelude to the collective agreement, he said.

"We got wages locked to December 1997, a tremendous advantage as labour wages consist of 55 percent of the cost of production," he said. "If that component can be accurately estimated, then one can make accurate financial projections."
The union has won wage hikes in the past by threatening strikes that could badly disrupt the plantation industry.
The union is politically powerful because its leadership has used its estimated 400,000 members as a bloc vote to help one or the other of Sri Lanka's two main political parties at general elections.

Harry Sandrasekera, the union's secretary of industrial relations, said that under a profit-sharing deal being negotiated, profits will trickle down to workers at times when commodity prices are strong.
"When prices go over an agreed threshold a percentage of the price on top of the threshold will go to the workers," he said.
The arrangement will be inoperative if prices fall below the threshold, he added.
"The CWC's main approach to bargaining is to ensure that while we safeguard the workers' interests, we do not destroy industry," Sandrasekera said. "Then nobody will benefit."
Seneviratne said the profit-sharing deal will be tied to productivity.
"Workers realise that plucking norms must be realistic and could vary according to the season," he said.

The Indian Ocean island is privatising its tea, rubber and coconut plantations, once the mainstay of its economy. Foreign companies are not allowed to control more than 49 percent of the regional plantation companies.
The once debt-ridden sector is recovering due to investments in replanting, fertiliser, machinery and value additions after privatisation.

Most of the 23 regional plantation firms that own some 600,000 hectares of tea, rubber and coconut had each run up debts ranging from five million rupees ($86,775) to 100 million rupees when the government began privatising their management in 1992, later followed by ownership.
Six firms, Kegalle Plantations, Kelani Valley Plantations, Agalawatte Plantations, Horana Plantations, Bogawantalawa Plantations and Kotagala Plantations, were privatised in 1995 and 1996.
Other companies are scheduled to be privatised this year.
